newsitem.title: FRANCE: France denies leukaemia problem near nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: France denies leukaemia problem near nuclear plant.

text.p: France on Friday dismissed a scientific report warning of an increased risk of leukaemia for children who played regularly on a beach near a nuclear processing plant.
The report "is not plausible and has no basis in science," the Industry, Post Office and Telecommunications Ministry said in a statement.

It said thousands of measurements taken in the area and in the marine life around the La Hague processing plant in Normandy had found radiation levels to be consistently lower than three percent of that of naturally occurring radiation in the environment.
The measurements, taken by France's Office for Protection against Ionising Radiation, are published monthly by the European Commission, the ministry said.

If France were to shut down its nuclear plants, which currently provide 75 percent of the nation's power needs, the pollution in the form of oxides of sulphur and nitrogen from conventional power plants would be a greater menace to health, the ministry statement added.

Writing earlier this month in the British Medical Journal, French government scientists Jean-Francois Viel and Dominique Pobel said their warning was based on 27 cases of leukaemia in people aged under 25 around the La Hague plant between 1978 and 1993.
"There is some convincing evidence in childhood leukaemia of a causal role for environmental radiation exposure from recreational activity on beaches," the French scientists said.
They called for more research to be carried out around La Hague as well as the Sellafield and Dounreay nuclear reprocessing plants in Britain.

The state-owned nuclear materials group Cogema (Compagnie generale des matieres nucleaires), which runs the Hague plant, said at the time that the scientists' survey was carried out on so small a group of individuals that its findings were baseless.
